title: God Hand: custom move strings, directional evasion and a difficulty meter that fights back
summary: Clover Studio stripped the 3D brawler down to close-range decisions, letting players build their own attack chain while enemy aggression rises or falls with performance.

sourceLabels.producer-interview: Interview: Atsushi Inaba on God Hand
sourceLabels.studio-interview: Capcom and Clover: Atsushi Inaba on a Post-Capcom World

blocks.text: The game committed to bodies, not weapons

God Hand focuses on punches, kicks, launches and evasions at intimate distance. Environments are comparatively plain because enemy pose, spacing and recovery need the player's attention. Shinji Mikami's team pursued the endangered arcade brawler rather than disguising it inside exploration. That narrow premise allowed unusually deep tuning of contact and response.
Players author the main attack string

Collected techniques can be assigned to the face buttons and arranged into a custom sequence. A quick jab, guard break, launcher or heavy finisher has different reach and recovery. Building a chain is therefore a practical design task: safe openers, situational properties and desired rhythm matter more than equipping a single weapon with a fixed moveset.
The right stick became an evasive language

Flicking the right stick produces slips, ducks and back movement instead of conventional camera control. The close camera follows Gene automatically, so the second stick can answer attacks with direction and timing. This feels restrictive to players expecting free camera movement, but it keeps offense and defense under separate hands and makes evasion immediate.
Cancels reward knowledge of animation boundaries

Many attacks can transition into movement, another technique or defensive action at useful moments. Mastery comes from learning which visual recovery is mandatory and which can be interrupted. The system keeps elaborate animations from becoming passive commitments, but poor timing remains punishable. Frame stability is essential because the player reads tiny windows inside rapid exchanges.
Difficulty rises when the player performs well

A visible level climbs from one toward DIE as Gene avoids damage and controls enemies. Higher levels make opponents more aggressive and dangerous while increasing rewards. Taking hits can reduce the pressure. The game therefore personalizes intensity during a run, not through hidden mercy alone, and lets experts deliberately maintain a harsher state.
Crowd control is the real arena

Enemies flank, interrupt and carry different threat ranges. Launches, knockbacks and brief invulnerability matter because focusing on one target can expose Gene to another. Small rooms and simple geometry make positioning legible. The challenge is not merely executing a long combo; it is deciding when the group permits that commitment.
God Reel and God Hand create controlled excess

Roulette techniques spend a limited resource on spectacular attacks, while releasing the God Hand enables a temporary burst of power. These systems provide recovery from a difficult crowd and support the game's absurd tone. Because they are limited, they do not replace the custom moveset; they punctuate a fight the player still has to manage.
Emulation errors change the combat design

Tests should verify input latency, analog-stick thresholds, animation speed, enemy physics and timing across 50 and 60 Hz releases. Frame-rate patches can alter combo windows or reactions if they change simulation speed. The camera should not be judged only by appearance: its automatic tracking is part of why directional evasion and enemy awareness work as designed.

God Hand initially divided reviewers because it looked sparse and rejected familiar camera conventions. Its coherence becomes clearer with practice. Custom offense, directional defense, cancel timing and dynamic pressure all ask the player to understand close combat rather than collect spectacle passively. The game is funny and deliberately abrasive, but the system beneath the jokes is exceptionally disciplined.
